notes.front: What is an Azure DevOps project?
notes.back: A space where users plan, track progress and collaborate on software; a basic container for data and source code.
notes.explanation: Creating a project also creates a team with the same name, which the documentation calls sufficient for small organisations.
notes.example: Fabrikam creates a "Web Shop" project to hold the backlog, code and pipelines for its online store.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “About projects and scaling your organization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A project in Azure DevOps provides a space for users to plan, track progress, and collaborate on building software solutions. It serves as a fundamental container for storing data and source code. When you create a project, Azure DevOps automatically creates a team with the same name, which is sufficient for small organizations.

notes.front: What is an Azure DevOps team?
notes.back: A group inside a project that gets its own configurable tools, such as backlogs, boards and dashboards.
notes.explanation: Organisations add teams as they grow, to manage specific products, services or feature areas.
notes.example: The Web Shop project has a Checkout team and a Catalogue team, each planning its own sprints.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create or add a team”, “Create or add a team” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: As your organization grows, add teams to manage specific products, services, or feature areas. Each new project includes a default team named after the project. Each team gets its own set of configurable tools: - Backlogs and boards - Sprint planning and capacity - Dashboards and alerts

notes.front: In Azure DevOps, what is a team administrator?
notes.back: A person with permission to add team members and configure all of a team's settings, including backlogs, boards and Taskboards.
notes.explanation: The documentation suggests making one or more users team administrators when a team is created.
notes.example: Priya, the Checkout team lead, is made its team administrator so she can set up its sprints and board.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create or add a team”, “Create a team and add team members” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Consider adding one or more users as team administrators. Team administrators have the necessary permissions to add team members and configure all team settings, including backlogs, boards, and Taskboards.

notes.front: What is an Azure DevOps security group?
notes.back: A group whose members inherit the permissions assigned to it; each permission either allows or denies a feature or task.
notes.explanation: Every Azure DevOps user belongs to one or more default security groups.
notes.example: Adding a new developer to a project's Contributors group gives her that group's permissions at once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All users in Azure DevOps belong to one or more default *security groups*. Assign *permissions* to security groups that either **Allow** or **Deny** access to features or tasks. - Members inherit the permissions assigned to their security group.

notes.front: What is the Project Collection Administrators group?
notes.back: The default group with broad administrative permissions over an organisation or collection, including creating and managing projects.
notes.explanation: Its members also manage the organisation's settings, policies and processes; Project Administrators work only at project level.
notes.example: The platform team that creates every new project for the company belongs to Project Collection Administrators.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Project Collection Administrators: - Have broad administrative permissions within an organization or project collection. - Manage settings, policies, and processes for the organization. - Create and manage projects. Project Administrators: - Operate at the project level.

notes.front: What is Stakeholder access in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: A free access level giving limited access to private projects; it can be assigned to any number of users without a licence.
notes.explanation: It is meant for people who need only a restricted set of features.
notes.example: A sales director who only reads and comments on work items is given Stakeholder access.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provides free, limited access to private projects. Stakeholders in existing public projects have broader access until those projects convert to private in 2027. Assign to an unlimited number of users without requiring a license or subscription, ideal for those needing access to a restricted set of features.

notes.front: What is a service principal in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: The security principal that represents an application in a Microsoft Entra tenant and defines its access policy and permissions there.
notes.explanation: Anything that needs access to resources a tenant secures must be a security principal: users are user principals, applications are service principals.
notes.example: Like a user account for a person, but it belongs to a program, such as a deployment tool that changes Azure resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Service principal object” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To access resources that are secured by a Microsoft Entra tenant, the entity that requires access must be represented by a security principal. This requirement is true for both users (user principal) and applications (service principal). The security principal defines the access policy and permissions for the user/application in the Microsoft Entra tenant.

notes.front: What is an application object in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: The single object that defines an application in the tenant where it was registered, used as a template for its service principals.
notes.explanation: The registering tenant is called the application's home tenant, and one application object can give rise to one or more service principals.
notes.example: A payroll app registered in Adatum's tenant has one application object there, even when other companies use it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Application object” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A Microsoft Entra application is defined by its one and only application object, which resides in the Microsoft Entra tenant where the application was registered (known as the application's "home" tenant). An application object is used as a template or blueprint to create one or more service principal objects.

notes.front: What is a managed identity in Azure?
notes.back: An identity assigned to an Azure compute resource that can then be authorised to access other resources, replacing secrets such as access keys.
notes.explanation: Once assigned, it can be authorised directly or indirectly to reach dependencies such as a storage account or database.
notes.example: A web app reads blobs from a storage account using its managed identity rather than a stored account key.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “What are managed identities?” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Once a managed identity is assigned on the compute resource, it can be authorized, directly or indirectly, to access downstream dependency resources, such as a storage account, SQL database, Cosmos DB, and so on. Managed identity replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords.

notes.front: What is a system-assigned managed identity?
notes.back: A managed identity enabled on one Azure resource; only that resource can use it, and its service principal shares the resource's life cycle.
notes.explanation: When the resource is deleted, Azure deletes the identity's service principal automatically.
notes.example: Switching on the identity setting of one virtual machine gives that machine an identity of its own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Managed identity types” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The service principal is tied to the lifecycle of that Azure resource. When the Azure resource is deleted, Azure automatically deletes the service principal for you. - By design, only that Azure resource can use this identity to request tokens from Microsoft Entra ID.

notes.front: What is a user-assigned managed identity?
notes.back: A managed identity created as a standalone Azure resource that you can assign to one or more Azure resources.
notes.explanation: Its service principal is managed separately from the resources that use it.
notes.example: An identity called build-reader is created in a resource group and later attached to an App Service app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Managed identity types” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can create a user-assigned managed identity and assign it to one or more Azure Resources. When you enable a user-assigned managed identity: - A service principal of a special type is created in Microsoft Entra ID for the identity. The service principal is managed separately from the resources that use it.

notes.front: What is an Azure DevOps personal access token (PAT)?
notes.back: An alternative password for Azure DevOps that identifies you and determines which resources and operations you can use.
notes.explanation: The documentation says to treat it with the same care as a password.
notes.example: A developer gives a command-line tool a PAT when it asks for Azure DevOps credentials.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Use personal access tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A personal access token (PAT) is an alternative password for Azure DevOps authentication. A PAT identifies you and determines the resources and operations available to you. Treat a PAT with the same care as a password.

notes.front: What is a service connection in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: An authenticated connection between Azure Pipelines and an external or remote service, used to run tasks in a job.
notes.explanation: Tasks in a pipeline job use the connection to reach the other service.
notes.example: A pipeline deploys to Azure through a connection called prod-azure that a project administrator set up once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage service connections”, “Manage service connections” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Service connections are authenticated connections between Azure Pipelines and external or remote services that you use to execute tasks in a job.

notes.front: What is an Azure Resource Manager service connection?
notes.back: A service connection that lets a pipeline connect to Azure resources and deploy to them without authenticating each time.
notes.explanation: An Azure App Service app is one example of a resource a pipeline can deploy to through it.
notes.example: A release pipeline uses the connection contoso-prod to deploy a web app into the production subscription.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect to Azure with an Azure Resource Manager service connection”, “Connect to Azure with an Azure Resource Manager service connection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This connection lets you use a pipeline to deploy to Azure resources, such as an Azure App Service app, without needing to authenticate each time.

notes.front: What is a workload identity federation service connection?
notes.back: An Azure Resource Manager service connection that uses workload identity federation with an app registration or managed identity, so it needs no secret.
notes.explanation: It is the option Microsoft recommends for connecting pipelines to Azure.
notes.example: A pipeline deploys to Azure through a connection backed by a user-assigned managed identity, with no client secret to rotate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect to Azure with an Azure Resource Manager service connection”, “Connect to Azure with an Azure Resource Manager service connection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We recommend using workload identity federation with either an app registration or managed identity. Workload identity federation eliminates the need for secrets and secret management.

notes.front: What is a job access token in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: A security token Azure Pipelines generates for each job at run time; the job's agent uses it to reach Azure DevOps resources.
notes.explanation: Because Azure Pipelines generates it at run time for each job, every job gets a token of its own.
notes.example: When a job checks out code from an Azure Repos repository, the agent authenticates with that job's token.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A job access token is a security token that is dynamically generated by Azure Pipelines for each job at run time. The agent on which the job is running uses the job access token in order to access these resources in Azure DevOps.

notes.front: What are the scoped build identities in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Two built-in identities that run pipelines: a collection-scoped identity for all projects and a project-scoped identity for one project.
notes.explanation: They are given the permissions pipelines need when calling back into Azure DevOps during a build or release.
notes.example: A nightly build runs under an identity Azure DevOps created, not under any person's account.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Scoped build identities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps uses two built-in identities to execute pipelines. A **collection-scoped identity**, which has access to all projects in the collection (or organization for Azure DevOps Services) A **project-scoped identity**, which has access to a single project These identities are allocated permissions necessary to perform build/release execution time activities when calling back to the Azure DevOps system.

notes.front: What is a GitHub App?
notes.back: An integration you build to interact with and extend GitHub, without signing in a user or creating a service account.
notes.explanation: GitHub describes it as a way to add flexibility and reduce friction in your processes.
notes.example: A bot that labels every new pull request is built as a GitHub App installed on the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About creating GitHub Apps”, “About GitHub Apps”
notes.evidence: is a type of integration that you can build to interact with and extend the functionality of {% data variables.product.company_short %}. You can build a {% data variables.product.prodname_github_app %} to provide flexibility and reduce friction in your processes, without needing to sign in a user or create a service account.

notes.front: What is the `GITHUB_TOKEN` in GitHub Actions?
notes.back: A unique token GitHub creates automatically at the start of each workflow job, used to authenticate within that job.
notes.explanation: Each job gets its own token, created as the job starts.
notes.example: A workflow step uses the token to post a comment on the pull request that triggered it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GITHUB_TOKEN”, “About the GITHUB_TOKEN”
notes.evidence: At the start of each workflow job, {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %} automatically creates a unique `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret to use in your workflow. You can use the `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate in the workflow job.

notes.front: What is a fine-grained personal access token on GitHub?
notes.back: A personal access token limited to one resource owner, optionally to chosen repositories, with specific fine-grained permissions.
notes.explanation: Its permissions offer more control than the scopes given to classic tokens.
notes.example: A token that can only read the contents of one repository in one organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing your personal access tokens”, “Fine-grained personal access tokens”
notes.evidence: Each token is limited to access resources owned by a single user or organization. Each token can be further limited to only access specific repositories for that user or organization. Each token is granted specific, fine-grained permissions, which offer more control than the scopes granted to

notes.front: What is a classic personal access token on GitHub?
notes.back: A GitHub personal access token granted broad scopes rather than fine-grained permissions, reaching every repository its owner can access.
notes.explanation: It covers all repositories in the owner's organisations and all repositories in the owner's personal account.
notes.example: A token with the repo scope that an old deployment script uses across many organisations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing your personal access tokens”, “Personal access tokens (classic)”
notes.evidence: keep in mind that it will grant access to all repositories within the organizations that you have access to, as well as all personal repositories in your personal account.

notes.front: What is the security manager role in a GitHub organisation?
notes.back: An organisation role that lets members view security alerts and manage security-feature settings across the organisation, with read access to every repository.
notes.explanation: Organisation owners can assign it to any member or team.
notes.example: The company's application security team is given the role so it can triage alerts in every repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, reusable text “about-security-managers” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/organizations/about-security-managers.md)
notes.evidence: The security manager role is an organization-level role that organization owners can assign to any member or team in the organization. When applied, it gives permission to view security alerts and manage settings for security features across your organization, as well as read permission for all repositories in the organization.

notes.front: Which two objects are created automatically in your home tenant when you register an application in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: An application object and a service principal object.
notes.explanation: Registering through the Microsoft Graph interfaces is different: creating the service principal is then a separate step.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Application registration” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you register an application, an application object and a service principal object are automatically created in your home tenant. If you register/create an application using the Microsoft Graph APIs, creating the service principal object is a separate step.

notes.front: What three aspects of an application does its application object describe?
notes.back: How tokens can be issued to access it, the resources it might need to access, and the actions it can take.
notes.explanation: Together they say how the application is reached, what it reaches and what it may do.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Application object” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The application object describes three aspects of an application: - How the service can issue tokens in order to access the application - The resources that the application might need to access - The actions that the application can take

notes.front: In which tenants is a service principal created for an application?
notes.back: In every tenant where the application is used.
notes.explanation: The application object is the blueprint from which those service principals are created.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Application object” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An application object is used as a template or blueprint to create one or more service principal objects. A service principal is created in every tenant where the application is used.

notes.front: Which type of service principal has no associated app object and can't be updated or modified directly?
notes.back: The managed identity type.
notes.explanation: It can still be granted access and permissions like other service principals.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Service principal object” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Service principals representing managed identities can be granted access and permissions, but can't be updated or modified directly. A service principal representing a managed identity doesn't have an associated app object (unlike the Application type above).

notes.front: Application object versus service principal: which is the global representation of an application and which the local one?
notes.back: The application object is global, used across all tenants; the service principal is local, used in one specific tenant.
notes.explanation: Each service principal takes its common and default properties from the application object, its template.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Relationship between application objects and service principals” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The application object is the global representation of your application for use across all tenants, and the service principal is the local representation for use in a specific tenant. The application object serves as the template from which common and default properties are derived for use in creating corresponding service principal objects.

notes.front: How many service principals does a single-tenant application have?
notes.back: One, in its home tenant, created and consented for use when the application is registered.
notes.explanation: A multitenant application also gets a service principal in each tenant where a user has consented to it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Relationship between application objects and service principals” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A single-tenant application has only one service principal (in its home tenant), created and consented for use during application registration. A multitenant application also has a service principal created in each tenant where a user from that tenant has consented to its use.

notes.front: Litware builds a multitenant timesheet app. Woodgrove's administrator consents to it for Woodgrove's tenant. What is created in Woodgrove's tenant?
notes.back: B) A service principal object for the app, with the permissions the administrator granted
notes.choices:
A) A copy of Litware's application object
B) A service principal object for the app, with the permissions the administrator granted
C) A new app registration owned by Woodgrove
D) A user-assigned managed identity for the app
notes.choicesExplained: A: the application object stays in the home tenant. C: consenting doesn't register the app again. D: managed identities are identities for Azure resources, not what consent creates.
notes.explanation: Consent gives each consuming tenant its own service principal for the app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Example” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When Contoso and Fabrikam administrators complete consent, a service principal object is created in their company's Microsoft Entra tenant and assigned the permissions that the administrator granted.

notes.front: What happens to the home-tenant service principal when you delete an application object?
notes.back: It is deleted too, and restoring the application object later does not restore it.
notes.explanation: Deleting affects both objects, but restoring through app registrations brings back only one of them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Consequences of modifying and deleting applications” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This means that deleting an application object will also delete its home tenant service principal object. However, restoring that application object through the app registrations UI won't restore its corresponding service principal.

notes.front: An app is under a security investigation. It must stop receiving new tokens, but its application object and service principal must be kept for later. What do you do?
notes.back: A) Deactivate the application
notes.choices:
A) Deactivate the application
B) Delete only the service principal
C) Delete the application object
D) Remove the app's redirect address
notes.choicesExplained: C also deletes the home-tenant service principal, and restoring the object won't bring it back. B removes an object you were asked to keep. D is not the documented way to suspend an app.
notes.explanation: Deactivation is meant for temporary suspension rather than permanent deletion.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “Consequences of modifying and deleting applications” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For applications that need temporary suspension rather than permanent deletion, you can deactivate the application. Deactivation prevents new token issuance while preserving the application object and service principal for investigation or future reactivation.

notes.front: Which Azure CLI command lists the service principals associated with an application?
notes.back: `az ad sp list --filter "appId eq '{AppId}'"`
notes.explanation: The filter selects service principals by the application's app ID.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Apps & service principals in Microsoft Entra ID”, “List service principals associated with an app” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: az ad sp list --filter "appId eq '{AppId}'"

notes.front: In Microsoft Entra, which three kinds of identity are workload identities?
notes.back: Applications, service principals and managed identities.
notes.explanation: Workload identities are one kind of machine, or non-human, identity; device identities are the other.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “What are managed identities?” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Machine / non-human identities consist of device and workload identities. In Microsoft Entra, workload identities are applications, service principals, and managed identities.

notes.front: Which two benefits of managed identities does Microsoft list?
notes.back: Any two of: no credentials to manage (you can't even see them), authentication to any resource supporting Microsoft Entra authentication, and no extra cost.
notes.explanation: The resources they can authenticate to include your own applications, if those support Microsoft Entra authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “What are managed identities?” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You don't need to manage credentials. Credentials aren’t even accessible to you. - You can use managed identities to authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications. - Managed identities can be used at no extra cost.

notes.front: Which type of managed identity does Microsoft recommend for Microsoft services?
notes.back: User-assigned managed identities.
notes.explanation: They are provisioned independently from compute and can be assigned to several compute resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Managed identity types” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: User-assigned managed identities, which are provisioned independently from compute and can be assigned to multiple compute resources, are the recommended managed identity type for Microsoft services.

notes.front: System-assigned versus user-assigned managed identity: how does each one's life cycle end?
notes.back: A system-assigned identity is deleted with its parent resource; a user-assigned one has an independent life cycle and must be deleted explicitly.
notes.explanation: Only the user-assigned kind outlives the resources that use it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Shared life cycle with the Azure resource that the managed identity is created with.
When the parent resource is deleted, the managed identity is deleted as well. | Independent life cycle.
Must be explicitly deleted.

notes.front: Can a system-assigned managed identity be shared across Azure resources, as a user-assigned one can?
notes.back: No. A system-assigned identity belongs to a single Azure resource; the same user-assigned identity can be associated with several.
notes.explanation: Sharing one user-assigned identity lets several resources act with the same identity.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Can’t be shared.
It can only be associated with a single Azure resource. | Can be shared.
The same user-assigned managed identity can be associated with more than one Azure resource.

notes.front: An application runs on a single virtual machine and needs an identity of its own. Which option matches Microsoft's documented use case?
notes.back: B) A system-assigned managed identity
notes.choices:
A) A user-assigned managed identity shared with other machines
B) A system-assigned managed identity
C) A service principal with a client secret
D) An Azure DevOps personal access token
notes.choicesExplained: A suits workloads spread over several resources that share one identity. C leaves a secret to manage. D authenticates to Azure DevOps, not to Azure resources.
notes.explanation: Workloads contained within one Azure resource, or needing independent identities, are the system-assigned use cases.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Workloads contained within a single Azure resource.
Workloads needing independent identities.
For example, an application that runs on a single virtual machine.

notes.front: Six virtual machines must all read the same storage account. The machines are rebuilt often, but their permissions must stay the same. Which option fits?
notes.back: D) One user-assigned managed identity assigned to all six machines
notes.choices:
A) A system-assigned managed identity on each machine
B) A classic personal access token
C) A job access token
D) One user-assigned managed identity assigned to all six machines
notes.choicesExplained: A gives each machine its own identity, deleted whenever that machine is. B is a GitHub credential, not an Azure identity. C is for pipeline jobs reaching Azure DevOps.
notes.explanation: Shared access and permissions that survive recycling are both listed user-assigned use cases.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Workloads where resources are recycled frequently, but permissions should stay consistent.
For example, a workload where multiple virtual machines need to access the same resource.

notes.front: A provisioning process must grant an identity access to a secure resource before the compute that will use it exists. Which option fits?
notes.back: C) A user-assigned managed identity
notes.choices:
A) A system-assigned managed identity
B) A Legacy service principal
C) A user-assigned managed identity
D) Stakeholder access
notes.choicesExplained: A is created as part of the resource itself. B represents old apps without an app registration. D is an Azure DevOps access level, not an Azure identity.
notes.explanation: Preauthorisation as part of a provisioning flow is a documented user-assigned use case.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Workloads needing preauthorization to a secure resource, as part of a provisioning flow.

notes.front: After creating a managed identity (and, if user-assigned, assigning it to the source resource), what are the next two steps?
notes.back: Authorise it to access the target service, then use it to access the resource.
notes.explanation: A user-assigned identity is first assigned to a source resource such as a virtual machine, logic app or web app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Use managed identity directly” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When using a user-assigned managed identity, you assign the managed identity to the "source" Azure Resource, such as a Virtual Machine, Azure Logic App or an Azure Web App. 1. Authorize the managed identity to have access to the "target" service. 1. Use the managed identity to access a resource.

notes.front: What is the name of a system-assigned managed identity's service principal?
notes.back: Always the same as the name of the Azure resource it was created for.
notes.explanation: For a deployment slot, the identity is named `<app-name>/slots/<slot-name>`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is managed identities for Azure resources?”, “Managed identity types” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The name of the system-assigned service principal is always the same as the name of the Azure resource it's created for. For a deployment slot, the name of its system-assigned managed identity is ```<app-name>/slots/<slot-name>```.

notes.front: Managed identity versus an app registration's service principal: who deals with the credentials?
notes.back: For a managed identity the Azure platform manages them; an app registration needs application credentials, a secret or certificate.
notes.explanation: Workloads running outside Azure are in the same position as app registrations and need such credentials.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Workload identity federation concepts”, “Why use workload identity federation?” (MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When these workloads run on Azure, you can use managed identities and the Azure platform manages the credentials for you. For a software workload running outside of Azure, or those running in Azure but use app registrations for their identities, you need to use application credentials (a secret or certificate) to access Microsoft Entra protected resources

notes.front: A script on an Azure virtual machine must read from a storage account, and the team wants no secret or password to store or rotate. What should the script authenticate as?
notes.back: A) A managed identity on the virtual machine
notes.choices:
A) A managed identity on the virtual machine
B) A service principal with a client secret
C) An Azure DevOps personal access token
