notes.explanation: The connection meets the conversion tool's conditions: Azure DevOps created it and one project uses it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect to Azure with an Azure Resource Manager service connection”, “Convert an existing service connection to use workload identity federation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can quickly convert an existing Azure Resource Manager service connection to use workload identity federation for authentication instead of a secret.

notes.front: Workload identity federation service connections that use the Azure DevOps issuer are deprecated and retire on {{c1::1 July 2027}}.
notes.explanation: The deprecated issuer is `https://vstoken.dev.azure.com`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Azure DevOps issuer deprecation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Workload identity federation service connections that use the Azure DevOps issuer (`https://vstoken.dev.azure.com`) are deprecated and will retire on July 1, 2027.

notes.front: Which issuer do new workload identity federation service connections use by default?
notes.back: The Microsoft Entra issuer, `https://login.microsoftonline.com/`.
notes.explanation: Existing connections flagged as deprecated should be converted to it before the retirement date.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Azure DevOps issuer deprecation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: New workload identity federation service connections use the Microsoft Entra issuer (`https://login.microsoftonline.com/`) by default. If your existing service connection is flagged as deprecated, convert it to the Microsoft Entra issuer before the retirement date.

notes.front: Which workload identity federation service connections are outside the Azure DevOps issuer deprecation?
notes.back: Those that target non-public clouds and those that use multitenant applications.
notes.explanation: Only public-cloud connections using single-tenant applications or managed identities are affected.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Azure DevOps issuer deprecation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This deprecation applies only to eligible service connections in Azure public cloud that use single-tenant Microsoft Entra applications or managed identities. Service connections that target non-public clouds and service connections that use multitenant applications are out of scope for this deprecation.

notes.front: A service connection in Azure public cloud that uses a single-tenant app is flagged as using the deprecated Azure DevOps issuer. What does Microsoft advise?
notes.back: D) Convert the existing connection to the Microsoft Entra issuer
notes.choices:
A) Switch the connection to a client secret
B) Ignore it, because only multitenant connections are affected
C) Create a replacement connection and delete the old one
D) Convert the existing connection to the Microsoft Entra issuer
notes.choicesExplained: B has it backwards: multitenant connections are the ones excluded. C replaces the connection, which the guidance says not to do. A moves back to a secret.
notes.explanation: Converting keeps the existing connection instead of replacing it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Azure DevOps issuer deprecation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you have an existing service connection that uses the Azure DevOps issuer, convert the existing connection instead of creating a replacement connection.

notes.front: If Azure DevOps can't update an identity automatically, which two values does it give you to create the federated credential yourself?
notes.back: The Issuer and the Subject identifier.
notes.explanation: You add the federated credential, in Azure or Microsoft Entra, on the identity linked to the service connection.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Use manual conversion when automatic conversion doesn't complete” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use the values shown in Azure DevOps to create the federated credential on the identity that's associated with the service connection. You need the following values from Azure DevOps: - **Issuer** - **Subject identifier**

notes.front: Why might someone who can edit a service connection still need an Azure administrator to finish a workload identity setup?
notes.back: Azure DevOps permissions and Azure permissions are separate; adding the federated credential needs rights in Azure or Microsoft Entra.
notes.explanation: The federated credential is added to the identity in Azure, outside Azure DevOps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Required permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps permissions and Azure permissions are separate. A user might be able to edit a service connection in Azure DevOps but still need help from an Azure administrator or identity owner to add the federated credential in Azure or Microsoft Entra.

notes.front: In a manually configured workload identity service connection, when is a managed identity more useful than an app registration?
notes.back: When you can't create service principals, or you use a different Microsoft Entra tenant from your Azure DevOps user.
notes.explanation: Either a managed identity or an app registration can do the authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection”, “Manually set an Azure Resource Manager workload identity service connection” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For authentication, you can use either a managed identity or an app registration. The managed identity option is useful if you don't have permissions to create service principals or if you're using a different Microsoft Entra tenant than your Azure DevOps user.

notes.front: What does Microsoft advise using instead of PATs for applications and automation?
notes.back: Microsoft Entra tokens, managed identities or service principals, whenever possible.
notes.explanation: Only if a tool can't use Microsoft Entra authentication should you fall back to an organisation-scoped PAT with minimal scopes and a short life.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Use personal access tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Avoid PATs when a more secure authentication method is available. For applications and automation, use Microsoft Entra tokens, managed identities, or service principals whenever possible. If a tool doesn't support Microsoft Entra authentication, use an organization-scoped PAT with the minimum scopes and shortest practical lifetime.

notes.front: All existing Azure DevOps global PATs stop working on {{c1::1 December 2026}}.
notes.explanation: They should be migrated to organisation-scoped PATs or Microsoft Entra authentication.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Use personal access tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps is retiring global PATs. All existing global PATs stop working on December 1, 2026. Migrate them now to organization-scoped PATs or Microsoft Entra authentication.

notes.front: An Azure DevOps PAT {{c1::can't grant more permissions than its owner has}}.
notes.explanation: The owner still needs the permissions for the resources and operations the PAT will be used for.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The permissions required for the resources and operations that the PAT accesses. A PAT can't grant more permissions than its owner has.

notes.front: After you create an Azure DevOps PAT, can you view its value again later?
notes.back: No. The token value doesn't appear again, so copy it and store it securely at once.
notes.explanation: Storing it in a secure location is part of the creation steps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Create a PAT” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select **Create**, copy the token, and store it in a secure location. The token value doesn't appear again.

notes.front: When creating an Azure DevOps PAT, which scopes should you select?
notes.back: Only the scopes required for the tasks the PAT is meant for.
notes.explanation: Microsoft's example is Agent Pools (Read & manage) for registering a self-hosted agent; administrators may also restrict full-scoped PATs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Create a PAT” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select only the scopes required for the intended tasks. For example, to register a self-hosted agent, select **Agent Pools (Read & manage)**. Your administrator might restrict full-scoped PATs or require an allow list entry for specific scopes.

notes.front: A reporting script only needs to read build results from one organisation. Which PAT should its owner create?
notes.back: A) An organisation-scoped PAT with only the build read scope and a short lifetime
notes.choices:
A) An organisation-scoped PAT with only the build read scope and a short lifetime
B) A full-scoped PAT, so it never lacks access
C) A global PAT that works in every organisation
D) A copy of a colleague's existing PAT
notes.choicesExplained: B grants far more than the task needs, and administrators may restrict full-scoped PATs. C: global PATs are being retired. D: Microsoft says not to share PATs.
notes.explanation: Minimal scopes and a short lifetime are both on Microsoft's list of PAT practices.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Create PATs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select only the scopes required for the task. - Keep the lifetime as short as practical.

notes.front: Nadia receives an email saying a PAT was created in her name. She didn't create it and doesn't recognise its name. What should she do?
notes.back: C) Revoke it and change her password
notes.choices:
A) Ignore it, because tools never create PATs
B) Regenerate it to get a fresh value
C) Revoke it and change her password
D) Extend its expiry so nothing breaks
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Git, App Service and Teams integrations can create PATs, but an unrecognised one should go. B and D keep the unknown token alive.
notes.explanation: With a Microsoft Entra account she should also ask an administrator to review unfamiliar sign-in activity.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Unexpected notification” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you don't recognize a PAT, [revoke it](#revoke-a-pat) and change your password. For a Microsoft Entra account, ask your administrator to review unfamiliar sign-in activity.

notes.front: For what does Microsoft say an Azure DevOps PAT is suitable, and for what not?
notes.back: Suitable for one-time requests, local prototypes or tools without Microsoft Entra support; not as long-term credentials for production applications or services.
notes.explanation: The line is drawn between short-lived experiments and production use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Use a PAT” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use a PAT for one-time requests, local prototypes, or tools that don't support Microsoft Entra authentication. Don't use PATs as long-term credentials for production applications or services.

notes.front: Does revoking an Azure DevOps PAT guarantee that every connection already using it ends?
notes.back: No. Later authentication attempts are rejected, but established connections aren't guaranteed to end.
notes.explanation: Pipelines, scripts and Git operations typically fail the next time they authenticate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Replace an expiring or revoked PAT” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After a PAT expires or is revoked, Azure DevOps rejects subsequent authentication attempts that use it. A pipeline, script, package client, or Git operation typically fails the next time it authenticates. Azure DevOps doesn't guarantee that revocation terminates every connection that is already established.

notes.front: What are two places where Microsoft says never to embed an Azure DevOps PAT?
notes.back: Any two of: Git remote URLs, `.git/config`, source code, pipeline `YAML` and logs.
notes.explanation: The value belongs in a secret store instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Rotate a PAT before it expires” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Store the new value in your secret store. Don't embed PATs in Git remote URLs, `.git/config`, source code, pipeline YAML, or logs.

notes.front: Where should an Azure Pipelines integration keep a PAT?
notes.back: In a secret variable, a variable group or a service connection.
notes.explanation: Git, by contrast, should use Git Credential Manager or another secure credential manager.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Rotate a PAT before it expires” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Git | Git Credential Manager or another secure credential manager | | Azure Pipelines | A secret variable, variable group, or service connection |

notes.front: Can the Azure DevOps audit log show when a PAT was last used?
notes.back: No. Token access events aren't currently logged; the log is for investigating lifecycle changes.
notes.explanation: It is meant for investigating lifecycle changes, not for tracking use.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Review PAT audit events” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Token access events aren't currently logged. Use the audit log to investigate lifecycle changes, not to determine when or whether a PAT was used.

notes.front: Which PAT policies can tenant administrators set, and where?
notes.back: Restrict global and full-scoped PATs, set a maximum lifetime and control leaked-PAT revocation, under Organization settings > Microsoft Entra.
notes.explanation: Organisation owners can separately restrict PAT creation for a single organisation under Organization settings > Policies.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Configure PAT policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Tenant administrators can restrict global PATs and full-scoped PATs, set a maximum PAT lifetime, and control automatic revocation of leaked PATs. Configure tenant-level PAT policies in **Organization settings** > **Microsoft Entra**. Organization owners can restrict PAT creation for an individual organization in **Organization settings** > **Policies**.

notes.front: Security wants no Azure DevOps PAT in the tenant to live longer than 30 days. Who can enforce this, and where?
notes.back: B) A tenant administrator, under Organization settings > Microsoft Entra
notes.choices:
A) Each user, when creating a PAT
B) A tenant administrator, under Organization settings > Microsoft Entra
C) A Project Administrator, under Project settings
D) A team administrator, in team settings
notes.choicesExplained: A relies on every user choosing well. C and D are project and team roles; PAT policies belong to tenant administrators and organisation owners.
notes.explanation: A maximum PAT lifetime is one of the tenant-level PAT policies.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Configure PAT policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Tenant administrators can restrict global PATs and full-scoped PATs, set a maximum PAT lifetime, and control automatic revocation of leaked PATs. Configure tenant-level PAT policies in **Organization settings** > **Microsoft Entra**.

notes.front: How long is an Azure DevOps PAT, and what fixed signature does it contain?
notes.back: 84 characters, 52 of them random, with the signature `AZDO` at positions 76 to 80.
notes.explanation: The identifiable format improves secret detection and reduces false positives.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “PAT format” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: PAT strings use an identifiable format that improves secret detection and reduces false positives. - PATs are 84 characters long, including 52 randomized characters. - Azure DevOps PATs contain the fixed `AZDO` signature at positions 76 through 80.

notes.front: A nightly service running in Azure calls Azure DevOps with a developer's PAT. Microsoft's guidance says to change this. What should it use?
notes.back: C) A managed identity or service principal with Microsoft Entra tokens
notes.choices:
A) The same PAT with a longer lifetime
B) A global PAT covering all organisations
C) A managed identity or service principal with Microsoft Entra tokens
D) A GitHub classic personal access token
notes.choicesExplained: A and B keep a person's token, and global PATs are being retired. D is a GitHub credential, not an Azure DevOps one.
notes.explanation: For applications and automation, Microsoft recommends Microsoft Entra tokens, managed identities or service principals.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use personal access tokens”, “Use personal access tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For applications and automation, use Microsoft Entra tokens, managed identities, or service principals whenever possible.

notes.front: From what two things are a job access token's permissions derived?
notes.back: The job authorisation scope, and the permissions set on the project or collection build service account.
notes.explanation: Controlling these is how you control which resources a pipeline can reach.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can control which resources your pipeline has access to by controlling how permissions are granted to job access tokens. The token's permissions are derived from (a) job authorization scope and (b) the permissions you set on project or collection build service account.

notes.front: Job authorisation scope: what can pipelines reach with collection scope, and with project scope?
notes.back: Collection: all repositories in the collection or organisation. Project: only repositories in the pipeline's own project.
notes.explanation: The scope is one of the two inputs to a job access token's permissions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Job authorization scope” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By setting the scope to **collection**, you choose to let pipelines access all repositories in the collection or organization. By setting the scope to **project**, you choose to restrict access to only those repositories that are in the same project as the pipeline.

notes.front: If the job authorisation scope isn't restricted at organisation or project level, what does every job in a `YAML` pipeline get?
notes.back: A collection-scoped job access token, which can reach any repository in any project of the organisation.
notes.explanation: One compromised pipeline could therefore reach every repository in the organisation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Job authorization scope” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the scope is not restricted at either the organization level or project level, then every job in your YAML pipeline gets a collection scoped job access token. In other words, your pipeline has access to any repository in any project of your organization.

notes.front: Someone who can edit a pipeline in one project might be an attacker. You want any breach contained to that project, for every project in the organisation. What do you do?
notes.back: A) Limit the job authorisation scope to the current project in Organization settings
notes.choices:
A) Limit the job authorisation scope to the current project in Organization settings
B) Limit it in some projects' settings only
C) Select Grant access permission to all pipelines on service connections
D) Add the build service accounts to Project Collection Administrators
notes.choicesExplained: B leaves any project you don't change open. C widens a service connection's use and doesn't touch the token's scope. D gives the build identity more power, not less.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends restricting the scope at the highest level, organisation settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Job authorization scope” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This is why, it is recommended that you restrict the scope at the highest level (organization settings) in order to contain the attack to a single project.

notes.front: What job authorisation scope applies to a pipeline in a public project?
notes.back: Project scope, automatically, whatever any setting says.
notes.explanation: Jobs there can reach build artifacts or test results only within their own project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Job authorization scope” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your pipeline is in a **public project**, then the job authorization scope is automatically restricted to **project** no matter what you configure in any setting. Jobs in a public project can access resources such as build artifacts or test results only within the project and not from other projects of the organization.

notes.front: What does the `Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines` setting do?
notes.back: Limits pipelines to Azure DevOps repositories explicitly referenced by a `checkout` step or `uses` statement in the job.
notes.explanation: Without it, pipelines can reach any Azure DevOps repository in authorised projects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pipelines can access any Azure DevOps repositories in authorized projects unless **Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines** is enabled. With this option enabled, you can reduce the scope of access for all pipelines to only Azure DevOps repositories explicitly referenced by a `checkout` step or a `uses` statement in the pipeline job that uses that repository.

notes.front: What is the name format of the collection-scoped build identity?
notes.back: `Project Collection Build Service ({OrgName})`.
notes.explanation: For an organisation called fabrikam-tailspin, it is `Project Collection Build Service (fabrikam-tailspin)`.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Scoped build identities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: name has the following format: - `Project Collection Build Service ({OrgName})` - For example, if the organization name is `fabrikam-tailspin`, this account has the name `Project Collection Build Service (fabrikam-tailspin)`.

notes.front: After you limit a pipeline to project scope, it can no longer restore packages from a feed in another project. What fixes this with the least extra access?
notes.back: A) Give the project's build service account access to that feed
notes.choices:
A) Give the project's build service account access to that feed
B) Return the whole organisation to collection scope
C) Give the pipeline author Stakeholder access
D) Store a developer's PAT in the pipeline
notes.choicesExplained: B undoes the protection for every pipeline. C is a person's access level, not the job's. D replaces the job's own token with a personal secret.
notes.explanation: Project scope may leave the project-scoped identity without permissions the collection-scoped one had.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access repositories, artifacts, and other resources”, “Manage build service account permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: One result of setting project-scoped access may be that the project-scoped identity may not have permissions to a resource that the collection-scoped one did have. You may want to change the permissions of job access token in scenarios such as the following: - You want your pipeline to access a feed that is in a different project.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is the difference between a permission and a role?
notes.back: A permission is the ability to perform one specific action; a role is a set of permissions you assign to people or teams.
notes.explanation: GitHub's example of a single permission is the ability to delete an issue.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, reusable text “about-roles” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/organizations/about-roles.md)
notes.evidence: A permission is the ability to perform a specific action. For example, the ability to delete an issue is a permission. A role is a set of permissions you can assign to individuals or teams.

notes.front: What does GitHub advise about the number of organisation owners?
notes.back: Keep the role limited, but to no fewer than two people.
notes.explanation: Owners have complete administrative access to the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization owners”
notes.evidence: Organization owners have complete administrative access to your organization. This role should be limited, but to no less than two people, in your organization.

notes.front: An application security team must see security alerts across all 300 repositories and change security-feature settings, without becoming organisation owners. Which role should they get?
notes.back: C) Security manager
notes.choices:
A) Organisation owner
B) Billing manager
C) Security manager
D) Write on every repository
notes.choicesExplained: A gives complete administrative access. B covers billing settings only. D is a repository role for people who push code, granted repository by repository.
notes.explanation: GitHub describes this role as giving a security team the least access it needs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Security managers”
notes.evidence: If your organization has a security team, you can use the security manager role to give members of the team the least access they need to the organization.

notes.front: Which repository role does GitHub recommend for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss a project?
notes.back: Read.
notes.explanation: Read is the role with the least access.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: From least access to most access, the roles for an organization repository are: * **Read:** Recommended for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss your project

notes.front: Which repository role suits contributors who proactively manage issues and pull requests but have no write access?
notes.back: Triage.
notes.explanation: It manages issues and pull requests without being able to push.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Recommended for contributors who need to proactively manage issues{% ifversion discussions-moderators-control-who-can-report %}, discussions,{% endif %} and pull requests without write access

notes.front: Which repository role does GitHub recommend for contributors who actively push to the project?
notes.back: Write.
notes.explanation: Pushing to the project is what this role is for.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Recommended for contributors who actively push to your project

notes.front: Which repository role suits project managers who manage the repository without sensitive or destructive actions?
notes.back: Maintain.
notes.explanation: It stops short of sensitive or destructive actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Recommended for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions

notes.front: Which repository role includes sensitive and destructive actions such as managing security or deleting the repository?
notes.back: Admin.
notes.explanation: It is the role with the most access, for people who need full access to the project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Recommended for people who need full access to the project, including sensitive and destructive actions like managing security or deleting a repository

notes.front: A project manager must manage a repository but must not delete it or change its security settings. Which repository role fits?
notes.back: A) Maintain
notes.choices:
A) Maintain
B) Admin
C) Triage
D) Write
notes.choicesExplained: D is for contributors who push code. B includes deleting the repository and managing security. C manages issues and pull requests only.
notes.explanation: Maintain is recommended for managing a repository without sensitive or destructive actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Recommended for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions

notes.front: What do base permissions set on a GitHub organisation?
notes.back: Access that applies to all members of the organisation when they use any of its repositories.
notes.explanation: Organisation owners are the ones who set them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”
notes.evidence: Organization owners can set base permissions that apply to all members of an organization when accessing any of the organization's repositories.

notes.front: Who can add an outside collaborator to a GitHub repository?
notes.back: People with admin access to that repository.
notes.explanation: Admin is the repository role that includes this.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Adding outside collaborators to repositories in your organization”, “Adding outside collaborators to repositories in your organization”
notes.evidence: People with admin access to a repository can add an outside collaborator to the repository.

notes.front: If an organisation requires two-factor authentication, what must an outside collaborator do?
notes.back: Enable two-factor authentication before accepting the invitation.
notes.explanation: The rule applies to every outside collaborator, not only to members.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Adding outside collaborators to repositories in your organization”, “About outside collaborators”
notes.evidence: If your organization requires two-factor authentication, all outside collaborators must enable two-factor authentication before accepting your invitation to collaborate on a repository.

notes.front: Can an outside collaborator be added to a team in the organisation?
notes.back: No. Team membership is restricted to members of the organisation.
notes.explanation: Outside collaborators get access repository by repository instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Adding outside collaborators to repositories in your organization”, “About outside collaborators”
notes.evidence: Outside collaborators cannot be added to a team, team membership is restricted to members of the organization.

notes.front: A freelance designer must push to one repository for three months without joining the organisation. What do you do?
notes.back: B) Add her as an outside collaborator on that repository
notes.choices:
A) Make her an organisation member with Write base permissions
B) Add her as an outside collaborator on that repository
C) Add her to the organisation's Designers team
D) Make her a billing manager
notes.choicesExplained: A makes her a member with access to every repository. C is impossible, because teams hold organisation members only. D grants billing settings, not repository access.
notes.explanation: Temporary people such as consultants are the documented fit for outside collaborators.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Outside collaborators”
notes.evidence: An outside collaborator is a person who has access to one or more organization repositories but is not explicitly a member of the organization, such as a consultant or temporary employee.

notes.front: Which Azure DevOps access level gives access to most features?
notes.back: Basic.
notes.explanation: It goes to Visual Studio Professional subscribers and to users for whom the organisation pays for Basic.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provides access to most features. Assign to users with a Visual Studio Professional subscription, an Azure DevOps Server CAL, and to users for whom you're paying for Basic access in an organization.

notes.front: Which Azure DevOps access level adds Azure Test Plans to everything in Basic?
notes.back: Basic + Test Plans.
notes.explanation: Visual Studio Test Professional subscribers are among those it is assigned to.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provides access to all features included in **Basic** and Azure Test Plans. Assign to users with a Visual Studio Test Professional or MSDN Platforms subscription

notes.front: Which access level should you give a new user who already has a Visual Studio subscription, and why?
notes.back: Visual Studio subscriber, so you aren't charged the Basic rate before the user first signs in.
notes.explanation: Choosing it instead of Basic avoids paying for Basic in the meantime.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: As a best practice when adding new users, assign the **Visual Studio Subscriber** level when appropriate (as opposed to Basic) to prevent being charged the **Basic** rate before the user signs in for the first time.

notes.front: A user assigned Stakeholder in Azure DevOps has a GitHub Enterprise licence. What access do they get?
notes.back: Basic access, regardless of the access level assigned.
notes.explanation: Azure DevOps recognises the licence the next time the user signs in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The system automatically recognizes users with a GitHub Enterprise license the next time they sign in to Azure DevOps. Regardless of a user's assigned access level (for example, they could be assigned **Stakeholder** access), they receive **Basic** access when they're associated with a GitHub Enterprise license.

notes.front: A developer's GitHub Enterprise licence expires. What might happen to her Azure DevOps access?
notes.back: D) It might drop to Stakeholder, restricting Azure Repos and Azure Pipelines
notes.choices:
A) Her PATs are revoked automatically
B) Nothing, because access levels never change once set
C) She becomes a member of Project Collection Administrators
D) It might drop to Stakeholder, restricting Azure Repos and Azure Pipelines
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores that her Basic access came from the licence. C is a security group, unrelated to licences. A confuses tokens with access levels.
notes.explanation: Without the licence her access can fall to Stakeholder, which restricts Azure Repos and Azure Pipelines.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started as a stakeholder”, “Get started as a stakeholder” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your Visual Studio subscription or GitHub Enterprise license expires, your Azure DevOps access might be limited to Stakeholder, restricting access to Azure Repos and Azure Pipelines.

notes.front: What can a Stakeholder do with release pipelines?
notes.back: View releases and act on approvals assigned to them, but not author release pipelines or manage releases.
notes.explanation: So a Stakeholder can approve a deployment without being able to change how it is defined.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Stakeholders can view releases and act on assigned approvals, but they can't author release pipelines or manage releases.

notes.front: What are two things Stakeholders can do in Azure Boards?
notes.back: Any two of: add and modify work items, view dashboards, and check project status.
notes.explanation: These let them give the team direction, feedback and business alignment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Get started as a stakeholder”, “Get started as a stakeholder” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can add and modify work items, view dashboards, and check project status to provide direction, feedback, and business alignment to your team.

notes.front: Forty business reviewers must view dashboards and comment on work items, and there is no licence budget. Which access level fits?
notes.back: B) Stakeholder
notes.choices:
A) Basic
B) Stakeholder
C) Visual Studio subscriber
D) Basic + Test Plans
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are paid levels with far more than they need. C is for people who already have a Visual Studio subscription.
notes.explanation: Stakeholder access is free for any number of users who need a restricted set of features.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Assign to an unlimited number of users without requiring a license or subscription, ideal for those needing access to a restricted set of features.

notes.front: How long do Stakeholders keep their broader access in existing public projects?
notes.back: Until those projects convert to private in 2027.
notes.explanation: In private projects, Stakeholder access is limited.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “Supported access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provides free, limited access to private projects. Stakeholders in existing public projects have broader access until those projects convert to private in 2027.

notes.front: Access levels versus security groups in Azure DevOps: what does each control?
notes.back: Access levels control which web portal features are available; security groups allow or deny specific tasks.
notes.explanation: Administrators use access levels so users get, and pay for, only the features they need.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About access levels”, “About access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Access levels in Azure DevOps control which web portal features are available. Access levels supplement security groups, which allow or deny specific tasks. Administrators ensure that their user base has access to the features they need and only pay for those specific features.

notes.front: At which levels can Azure DevOps permissions be defined?
notes.back: Organisation or collection, project, and object.
notes.explanation: Some permissions are managed through role-based assignments instead, such as team administrator.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Define permissions at different levels: organization/collection, project, or object. - Manage some permissions through *role-based assignments* (for example, team administrator, extension management, or pipeline resource roles).

notes.front: Which group should people join to manage projects, policies, processes, retention policies, agent pools and extensions?
notes.back: Project Collection Administrators.
notes.explanation: These are organisation or collection-level features.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Default security groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add users who manage organization or collection-level features to the **Project Collection Administrators** group. These features include projects, policies, processes, retention policies, agent and deployment pools, and extensions.

notes.front: Which group should people join to manage a project's teams, area and iteration paths, repositories, service hooks and service endpoints?
notes.back: Project Administrators.
notes.explanation: These are project-level features, unlike the organisation-level ones Project Collection Administrators manage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Default security groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add users who manage project-level features to the **Project Administrators** group. These features include teams, area and iteration paths, repositories, service hooks, and service endpoints.

notes.front: Which group should a person join to create new projects in the organisation?
notes.back: B) Project Collection Administrators
notes.choices:
A) Project Administrators
B) Project Collection Administrators
C) Contributors
D) Readers
notes.choicesExplained: A works within a single project. C gives read and write access to project resources. D is not an administrative group.
notes.explanation: Creating and managing projects is an organisation-level task.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Project Collection Administrators: - Have broad administrative permissions within an organization or project collection. - Manage settings, policies, and processes for the organization. - Create and manage projects.

notes.front: Which security group and access level do most Azure DevOps users get?
notes.back: The Contributors group and the Basic access level.
notes.explanation: Contributors get read and write access to repositories, work tracking, pipelines and more.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Default security groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Most Azure DevOps users are added to the **Contributors** security group and granted the **Basic** access level. The **Contributors** group provides read and write access to repositories, work tracking, pipelines, and more.

notes.front: Which Azure DevOps permission states can't you edit?
notes.back: Allow (system) and Deny (system).
notes.explanation: Azure DevOps itself manages these permissions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Allow (system)**   |Grants a permission that Azure DevOps manages. You can't edit system permissions.

notes.front: What does the Not set permission state do?
notes.back: It neither grants nor denies the permission; other applicable assignments decide the effective permission.
notes.explanation: It leaves the decision to the other assignments that apply.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Neither grants nor denies the permission at the current scope. Other applicable assignments determine the effective permission.

notes.front: Allow versus Allow (inherited): where does each come from?
notes.back: Allow is granted explicitly at the current scope; Allow (inherited) comes through a parent scope or group membership.
notes.explanation: Inherited values arrive through a parent scope or a group the user belongs to.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Explicitly grants the permission to the selected user or group at the current scope.         | |**Allow (inherited)**    |Grants the permission through a parent scope or group membership.

notes.front: At the same scope, one of a user's groups allows a permission and another denies it. Which usually wins?
notes.back: Deny generally takes precedence over Allow.
notes.explanation: Otherwise users receive the combined permissions of all the groups they belong to.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Users receive the combined permissions of the groups they belong to. - At the same scope, a **Deny** from one group generally takes precedence over an **Allow** from another group.

notes.front: A group is explicitly denied a permission on the Payments area path but explicitly allowed it on Payments/Refunds. What applies to that group on Payments/Refunds?
notes.back: A) Allow, because the explicit setting on the child replaces the inherited value
notes.choices:
A) Allow, because the explicit setting on the child replaces the inherited value
B) Deny, because Deny always wins
C) Not set
D) Deny (system)
notes.choicesExplained: B: Deny generally wins when assignments are combined at the same scope, not over an explicit setting on a child node. C: a value is explicitly set. D: system states are managed by Azure DevOps, not set by you.
notes.explanation: An explicit setting on a subnode replaces the value that identity inherits from the parent.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If a permission is explicitly set for an identity on a subnode, the value inherited from the parent for that identity doesn't apply on the subnode.

notes.front: What happens to an object-level permission set on a higher-level node, such as an area path?
notes.back: All subnodes inherit it unless it is explicitly overridden.
notes.explanation: Object-level permissions go on nodes such as areas, iterations, version control folders and query folders.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You assign object-level permissions to nodes like areas, iterations, version control folders, and work item query folders. These permissions are inherited down the hierarchy. **Object hierarchy rules:** - Permissions set at a higher-level node get inherited by all subnodes unless explicitly overridden.

notes.front: Why does Microsoft warn you to take care when changing a permission for a group?
notes.back: The change affects every user in the group, possibly hundreds of people.
notes.explanation: Consider the potential effects before making any adjustment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Permission states” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you modify a permission for a group, it affects all users in that group. Even a single permission change can impact hundreds of users, so consider the potential effects before making any adjustments.

notes.front: What does Azure DevOps create automatically for each team you add?
notes.back: A security group for that team, which you can use to manage the team's permissions.
notes.explanation: The group lets you manage permissions for the team as a whole.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Structure your project” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each team you create automatically creates a security group for that team, which you can use to manage permissions for a team.

notes.front: Why does Microsoft suggest filling Azure DevOps security groups from Microsoft Entra ID rather than one user at a time?
notes.back: For ease of management: it is more efficient than adding individual users.
notes.explanation: Adding individual users still works; the Microsoft Entra approach is simply easier to manage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Active Directory and Microsoft Entra security groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can populate security groups by adding individual users. But, for ease of management, it's more efficient to populate these groups using Microsoft Entra ID for Azure DevOps Services

notes.front: Which organisation preview feature stops chosen users seeing projects they haven't been added to?
notes.back: Limit user visibility and collaboration to specific projects, which applies to the Project-Scoped Users group.
notes.explanation: It also limits those users' access to organisation settings and to identities in people pickers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Project-scoped users group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable this feature, users and groups in the **Project-Scoped Users** group can access only the projects to which you explicitly add them. The feature also limits their access to organization settings and identities in people pickers.

notes.front: Guest users from a partner company must see only the one project they work in, not the rest of the organisation. What do you enable?
notes.back: A) Limit user visibility and collaboration to specific projects
notes.choices:
A) Limit user visibility and collaboration to specific projects
B) Stakeholder access for the guests
C) Public visibility for the project
D) A Deny on View project-level information for Project Valid Users
notes.choicesExplained: B limits features, not which projects they can see. C opens the project wider. D changes a Valid Users group's defaults, which can block every member of that group.
notes.explanation: Microsoft Entra guest users are one of the groups this preview feature is meant to restrict.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About permissions and security groups”, “Project-scoped users group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To restrict specific users, such as Stakeholders, Microsoft Entra guest users, or members of a particular security group, you can enable the **Limit user visibility and collaboration to specific projects** preview feature for the organization.

notes.front: Azure DevOps supports up to {{c1::1,000}} projects within an organisation.
notes.explanation: Enterprise-level organisations may need to scale up by creating more teams and projects.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “About projects and scaling your organization” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For enterprise-level organizations, you might need to scale up by creating more teams and projects. Azure DevOps supports up to 1,000 projects within an organization.

notes.front: What does Microsoft say a single project can do for an organisation?
notes.back: Minimise administrative maintenance and give the most optimised, flexible cross-linking of objects.
notes.explanation: It is one recommended way to support a whole organisation or enterprise.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Use a single project” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: One recommended approach is to use a single project to support your organization or enterprise. A single project can help minimize the maintenance of administrative tasks and provides the most optimized and flexible cross-link object experience.

notes.front: What is lost when data is moved from one Azure DevOps project to another?
notes.back: The associated history.
notes.explanation: Each project isolates the data stored within it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Use a single project” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A project isolates the data stored within it, and moving data from one project to another results in the loss of associated history.

notes.front: What are two reasons Microsoft gives for using more than one project?
notes.back: Among others: restricting access to a project's information for some groups, and separate business units with their own administrators.
notes.explanation: Custom work tracking processes and testing customisations before rollout are further reasons.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Add another project” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Prohibit or manage access to the information contained within a project for select groups - Support custom work tracking processes for specific business units within your organization - Support entirely separate business units that have their own administrative policies and administrators - Test customization activities or add extensions before rolling out changes to the working project

notes.front: A subsidiary with its own administrators and its own work-tracking process joins the company's Azure DevOps organisation. How should its work be structured?
notes.back: C) In a project of its own
notes.choices:
A) As a new team in the main project
B) As an area path in the main project
C) In a project of its own
D) By giving its staff Stakeholder access in the main project
notes.choicesExplained: A and B keep it inside a project whose administration and process it doesn't share. D only changes which features its staff can use.
notes.explanation: Separate administrative policies and custom work-tracking processes are both listed reasons for another project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Add another project” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Support custom work tracking processes for specific business units within your organization - Support entirely separate business units that have their own administrative policies and administrators

notes.front: Private versus public projects: which kind lets people use many services read-only without signing in?
notes.back: Public projects; private projects need sign-in even for read-only access.
notes.explanation: Public projects also support sharing code and continuous integration and deployment of open-source software.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About projects and scaling your organization”, “Use private and public projects” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Public projects**: - Don't require users to sign in for read-only access to many services. - Support sharing code with others. - Support continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) of open-source software.

notes.front: What default team does a new project called Northwind get?
notes.back: A team called Northwind, with backlogs, boards and dashboards already set up.
notes.explanation: Having those tools ready lets the team start defining work items straight away.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About teams and Agile tools”, “The default team” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each new project is configured with a default team named after the project. For example, the *Fabrikam* project is automatically configured with the *Fabrikam* team. Backlogs, boards, and dashboards are set up for this default team, allowing you to start defining work items and your backlog immediately.

notes.front: A project called Tailspin Toys has just been created. Before anyone sets up teams, the product owner wants to start adding backlog items. What can she use?
notes.back: B) The backlog of the Tailspin Toys team, which already exists
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, until a Project Administrator creates a team
B) The backlog of the Tailspin Toys team, which already exists
C) A backlog that comes with Stakeholder access
D) An organisation-wide backlog shared by all projects
notes.choicesExplained: A: a default team named after the project is created automatically. D: backlogs belong to teams. C: Stakeholder is an access level, not a backlog.
notes.explanation: Every new project gets a default team named after it, with its backlog ready.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About teams and Agile tools”, “The default team” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Backlogs, boards, and dashboards are set up for this default team, allowing you to start defining work items and your backlog immediately.

notes.front: At roughly what size does Microsoft suggest you might move from one team to two?
notes.back: When the team grows beyond its intended size, typically 6 to 9 members.
notes.explanation: A hierarchical team structure then helps managers track progress across teams.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About teams and Agile tools”, “About teams and Agile tools” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When your team grows beyond its intended size—typically anywhere from 6-to-9 members—you might consider moving from a one-team structure to a two-team structure. You can then set up a hierarchical team structure, which provides several advantages to managers for tracking progress across teams.

notes.front: What permissions do Azure DevOps team members get by default?
notes.back: Those of the project's Contributors group.
notes.explanation: That covers changing source code, test runs and work items.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About teams and Agile tools”, “Team member permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, team members inherit the permissions afforded to members of the project Contributors group. Members of this group can add and modify source code, create and delete test runs, and create and modify work items.

notes.front: What determines which work items appear on a team's backlogs and boards?
notes.back: The team's area paths and iteration paths.
notes.explanation: When work items are added to a backlog or board, the team's defaults fill in their field values.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About teams and Agile tools”, “Team defaults referenced by backlogs and boards” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Work items that appear on team backlogs and boards are determined by the team's *area paths* and *iteration paths*. When you add work items to a backlog or board, team defaults are used to assign field values.

notes.front: Who can create a team, and who can add its members or configure it?
notes.back: Creating: Project Administrators. Adding members or configuring: the team administrator or a Project Administrator.
notes.explanation: Configuring a team doesn't require membership of Project Administrators.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create or add a team”, “Prerequisites” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
**Create a team**: Member of the [Project Administrators](../security/change-project-level-permissions.md) group.
- **Add members or configure a team**: [Team administrator](add-team-administrator.md) or member of the [Project Administrators](../security/change-project-level-permissions.md) group.

notes.front: Which Azure DevOps CLI command creates a team?
notes.back: `az devops team create --name <name>`
notes.explanation: Optional arguments set the description and the project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create or add a team”, “Create a team and add team members” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: az devops team create --name [--description] [--project]

notes.front: The Search team's lead must add team members and change the team's board settings, but must not manage project security. What do you grant?
notes.back: A) Team administrator of the Search team
notes.choices:
A) Team administrator of the Search team
B) Membership of Project Collection Administrators
C) Membership of Project Administrators
D) Stakeholder access
notes.choicesExplained: C and B include project-wide or organisation-wide administration. D is a free, limited access level that adds no team settings rights.
notes.explanation: Team administrators can add members and configure all team settings, including backlogs and boards.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create or add a team”, “Create a team and add team members” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Team administrators have the necessary permissions to add team members and configure all team settings, including backlogs, boards, and Taskboards.
